Payments & Understanding
How to Pay Property Taxes
Ways to pay your property tax:
Online by eCheck ($0.75 fee) or card (2.35% fee, with a minimum fee of $1.49)
Pay Online
Mail (check and payment stub) to Washington County Taxpayer Services, 14949 62nd St. N., P.O. Box 200, Stillwater, MN 55082-0200 Must be postmarked by the due date to avoid penalties
Bill pay through your bank
Secure drop box or In-person at the Government Center in Stillwater or any Washington County Service Center
Visit Government Center in Stillwater
Visit Washington County Service Centers
Understanding Your Property Taxes
How are property taxes determined?
Property taxes do not have a set rate like income or sales taxes. With property taxes, taxing jurisdictions determine the dollar amount to raise from property taxes. This is called the “levy.” The levy is divided by the total value of the property in the taxing jurisdiction, the “tax base,” to arrive at a tax rate. The tax rate is multiplied by the value of each individual parcel to determine each parcel’s share of property taxes.
If my value went up 20%, will my tax go up 20%?
A value increase does not correlate directly to an increase in property tax. Property value is only one factor that is used to determine the portion of property tax each property owner pays.
Does an increase in property value mean the government will get more money?
Increases in values do not generate more tax revenue. Only an official action by a taxing authority to increase the tax levy will increase the total amount collected and only the amount levied can be collected.
What should I do if I feel my assessed market value or classification are incorrect?
Call 651-430-6175 to talk to an assessor.
Additional Information on Assessments and Values
Why do I have a homestead exclusion this year? Was there a recent change?
The Homestead Market Value Exclusion is increased starting with taxes payable in 2025. The market value exclusion reduces the taxable market value of homestead property. The exclusion decreases as the value increases and the exclusion increases as the value decreases.
View Homestead Market Value Exclusion Impacts (PDF)
Understanding Property Tax | Minnesota Department of Revenue (External)
Property Tax Notices
Step 1. Valuation Notices
The county mails Property Tax Statements by March 31 for the current year. The envelope also includes a Notice of Valuation and Classification for next year’s taxes.
Access your statement online with your property ID or address.
Search for your statement online
View a description of line items on your statement.
View Description of Line Items (PDF)
The valuation notice shows:
Estimated market value of your property
Property classification
Information about the Local Board of Appeals and Equalization
The property is assessed on January 2 and sets the basis for next year’s taxes. For example, a valuation notice mailed in March 2026 is used for 2027 taxes.
Step 2. Proposed Property Tax Notice
The county mails your Proposed Property Tax Notice (also called the “Truth in Taxation” notice) in mid-November .
The Proposed Property Tax Notice shows an estimate of the property tax you may pay the next year if local budgets are approved.
Property owners can attend public budget meetings to share input on local taxes.
Step 3. Property Tax Statement
The property tax statement is mailed in March after taxing districts set levies. The statement includes the final taxes and includes a Valuation Notice for the next year.
How Property Taxes Are Calculated
Property taxes are not a fixed rate like income or sales taxes.
Levy: Each taxing jurisdiction decides the total amount of money to collect from property taxes.
Tax rate : The levy is divided by the total property value in the jurisdiction to determine a tax rate.
Your tax: Your parcel’s value is multiplied by the tax rate.
Taxes may increase even if property values decrease. Factors that affect your tax include:
Spending decisions (levy) of each taxing jurisdiction
Changes in total property values (tax base) in the jurisdiction
Changes in your property’s value
How your property value change compared to others
Changes due to homestead classification
Estimate taxes: Use the interactive calculator to estimate taxes for homestead, non-homestead, apartment, or commercial/industrial properties.
Visit the Interactive Calculator
School District Taxes: School taxes include voter-approved levies and other local levies. Contact your school district for details. Proposed property tax notices do not include voter-approved referendums.
Property Tax Refunds
Property Tax Refunds
If you own and live in your property as your homestead , you may qualify for one or both of the following refunds through the State of Minnesota:
Property Tax Refund : Sometimes called the "circuit breaker," this refund is based on household income and the amount of property tax you pay. Minnesota homeowners with a 2025 total household income under $142,490 may qualify for the 2025 homestead credit refund.
Learn More: Homestead Credit Refund
Special Homestead Credit Refund : To qualify, your net property tax must increase by at least 12 percent and by at least $100 from one year to the next. The special refund is not based on income. Increases caused by property improvements do not qualify.
Forms and instructions are available on the Minnesota Department of Revenue website.
Visit the Minnesota Department of Revenue
Businesses can contact the Washington County Community Development Agency for help with property taxes.
Visit the Washington County Community Development Agency
Delinquent and Unpaid Taxes
What happens if property taxes are not paid?
Monthly penalties begin to accrue if property taxes are not paid by the due date. Penalty rates are listed on the back of the tax statement and increase each month the payment remains late.
Unpaid taxes become delinquent on January 2 of the following year. At that time:
Penalty rates increase.
Interest begins accruing on the unpaid tax, penalties, and fees at an annual rate of 8%, increasing monthly.
Due Dates
Most property taxes are due in two equal installments on May 15 and October 15.

Delinquent Property Taxes
Delinquent Tax Proceedings
Each year, the county starts delinquent tax proceedings for newly delinquent properties. Property owners are notified, typically in March, through:
A letter mailed to the property owner.
Publication of the Delinquent Tax List in the newspaper for two consecutive weeks.
View Delinquent Tax List (PDF)
This list includes parcel number, owner name, address, property description, and delinquent amount.
As payments may be made after publication, property owners should verify the current status online or by phone. Payment plans may be available depending on property classification.
A delinquency fee of $25 is added to cover publication and notification costs.
Redemption Period
The first year of delinquency begins the three-year redemption period. (Prior to 2014, some property types had a five-year redemption period.)
To redeem a property and avoid forfeiture, you must pay the delinquent taxes, penalties, interest, and fees within this period.
If taxes are not paid by the end of the redemption period, the property forfeits to the State of Minnesota.
View Example of Calculation (PDF)
Notice of Forfeiture
If taxes remain unpaid at the end of the redemption period, the property forfeits to the State of Minnesota. The county typically sends a courtesy notice in October of the year before forfeiture. Formal notice, usually in April, includes:
Certified mail to the property owner.
Publication of the Expiration of Redemption list in the county appointed newspaper for two weeks. As payments may occur after publication, owners should confirm the current status online or by phone.
The Expiration of Redemption list is posted in the office of Property Records and Taxpayer Services.
The sheriff serves a copy of the notice to an occupant.
A fee of $150 is imposed to cover publication, notification, and sheriff service costs.
For properties with redemption expiring in 2026, payment must be received by July 17, 2026, to avoid forfeiture.
Confession of Judgment Payment Plan
A Confession of Judgment (COJ) is a way to repay delinquent property taxes over time and avoid tax forfeiture. Payments for the total delinquent amount (taxes, penalties, special assessments, costs, and accrued interest) are made in equal annual installments. To be eligible, you must have a legal interest in the property as one of the following:
Property owner
Lender
Buyer under a Contract for Deed
Holder of a Life Estate
Power of Attorney for any eligible party listed above
